title: The Government Says Satluj Bypassed the Censor Board. The Real Story Is Messier.
excerpt: India has formed a high-level committee to review Diljit Dosanjh's banned film — after the Ministry accused filmmakers of dodging 127 cuts by changing the title and going straight to OTT. For NRIs, the film is still streaming.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The Indian government formed a committee to review the banned film *Satluj*.
  • Filmmakers bypassed 127 cuts by changing the title and releasing on OTT.
  • The film is still available for NRIs outside India despite domestic bans.
  • Diljit Dosanjh highlighted the film's impact, even after its takedown.
  • The case raises questions about OTT freedom and censorship in India.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=T8hpgSsSDPQ

Two days after pulling Diljit Dosanjh's *Satluj* from ZEE5, the Indian government isn't backing down. It's escalating.

The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has constituted a high-level Inter-Departmental Committee (IDC) under Rule 14 of the IT Rules, 2021, to formally examine the film's content. The committee's findings will determine whether *Satluj* can return to Indian screens — or whether further action is warranted. "Further action" is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence.

But the Ministry also did something else. It accused the filmmakers of deliberately bypassing the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) — and the accusation is explosive.

The 127 Cuts

Here's the timeline the Ministry laid out: the film was originally submitted to the CBFC in 2022 under its original title, Punjab 95. The censor board didn't just object. It demanded 127 cuts — an unprecedented number that effectively gutted the movie. The filmmakers fought back in court. They lost. They renamed the film *Satluj*, skipped the censor board entirely, and released it directly on ZEE5 with every second of the original footage intact. Zero cuts.

> ""Further action" is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence."

The Ministry's argument? OTT platforms don't fall under the CBFC's jurisdiction — they're regulated under Part III of the IT Rules instead. By changing the title and going directly to streaming, the filmmakers exploited that gap. Nobody from the production team, the Ministry claims, reached out for any kind of approval before the film went live.

It's a clever legal argument. It's also a terrifying precedent.

The Film That Wouldn't Die

*Satluj* is based on the life of Jaswant Singh Khalra, a human rights activist who documented the extrajudicial cremation of over 25,000 Sikhs in Punjab between 1984 and 1994. Khalra was abducted by Punjab Police in 1995 and never seen again. Diljit plays him with a quiet, simmering fury that reviewers have called his finest screen work. Directed by Honey Trehan and co-starring Arjun Rampal, the film had been stuck in certification limbo for nearly four years before its OTT breakout.

The CBFC's 127 cuts — if implemented — would have stripped virtually every reference to the state's involvement in the killings. The film would have been about nothing.

Diljit's response was devastating. Before the takedown even came, he told fans during an online interaction that *Satluj* was meeting "the same fate as the late Khalra saab." When it happened, he didn't rage. He pointed out that people had already downloaded it, that it was being projected on screens at gurdwaras across Punjab, and that the work had reached its audience the way it was always meant to.

> "People have downloaded it. What made me happiest was seeing folks screen the movie on projectors at Gurudwara Sahib. It brought me real joy." — Diljit Dosanjh

ZEE5 issued a measured statement, calling the audience response "truly overwhelming" and pledging to explore "every appropriate avenue through due process" to restore the film. The platform's social media was sharper: "Satluj may have paused. But the conversation it started hasn't."

Why This Matters for NRIs

Here's the detail that makes this a distinctly diaspora story: the film is still streaming outside India. If you're in the US, UK, Canada, or anywhere beyond Indian borders, *Satluj* remains available on ZEE5 International. The government's order applies only domestically.

That creates a strange split. The film India's censors decided Indian audiences shouldn't see is freely available to the Indian diaspora — the very community most likely to have personal, family connections to the events it depicts. For many NRIs with roots in Punjab, this isn't entertainment. It's memory.

Impact Beyond Borders
›Available for NRIs in US, UK, Canada.
›Domestic ban does not affect international streaming.
›Film resonates deeply with Punjabi diaspora.
›Highlights disparity in censorship for domestic vs. international audiences.

The broader question *Satluj* now forces is one the Indian entertainment industry has been dodging for years: what is OTT freedom, really? If a film rejected by the CBFC can simply rename itself and premiere on a streaming platform, the censor board becomes irrelevant. If the government can pull any OTT title on "security grounds" without judicial review, streaming becomes just as constrained as theatres ever were.

The IDC committee's verdict will determine which version of that future India chooses. For now, Khalra's story is doing exactly what it always did — surviving attempts to silence it.
